note.explanation: An electromagnet is made when electric current passes through a coil around an iron object. It acts as a magnet while current flows. Electromagnets are useful because their magnetism can be switched on and off.
examples: An iron nail inside a current-carrying coil can attract paper clips.
A scrapyard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift iron and steel, then releases them when the current is switched off.
note.checkAnswer: A circuit breaker uses an electromagnet to attract an armature. If the current is excessive, the armature detaches from the copper strip and breaks the circuit.
note.simple: A coil carrying current can make an iron nail magnetic. Turn off the current and the nail stops acting as a magnet.
note.checkQuestion: What happens in a circuit breaker when the current becomes excessive?
note.title: Electromagnets: magnets made by current
steps: Wind a covered copper wire around an iron nail to make a coil.
Connect the coil to a battery through a switch.
Switch on the current: the nail becomes a magnet and can attract clips.
Switch off the current: the nail no longer remains a magnet.
note.answer: The nail or rod becomes a magnet when electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet.

options: It becomes a magnet only while current passes through the coil.
It remains a magnet permanently after the current stops.
It becomes magnetic only when the switch is off.
It cannot attract iron objects.
mcqs.stem: An iron nail is placed inside a coil connected to a battery. What happens when current flows?
rationales: Correct: current through the coil magnetizes the iron nail, which acts as a temporary magnet.
Incorrect: the section says the iron object no longer remains a magnet when current stops.
Incorrect: the nail becomes magnetized when current passes, not when the switch is off.
Incorrect: the magnetized nail can attract objects such as paper clips.

options: The nail becomes a permanent magnet.
The nail no longer remains a magnet.
The coil stops having any wire turns.
The battery changes into a magnet.
mcqs.stem: What happens to an electromagnet's iron core when the current is stopped?
rationales: Incorrect: the section describes the iron object as remaining a magnet only while current passes.
Correct: when the current is stopped, the iron object no longer remains a magnet.
Incorrect: switching off current does not change the number of turns of wire.
Incorrect: the battery is not described as becoming a magnet.

options: Increase the number of cells or the number of coil turns.
Reduce the number of cells and coil turns.
Remove the iron core and switch off the current.
Use fewer turns and a lower current.
mcqs.stem: Which change can increase the strength of an electromagnet?
rationales: Correct: increasing the number of cells or coil turns increases the magnetic field strength.
Incorrect: reducing cells and turns does not produce the increase described in the section.
Incorrect: removing the core and switching off current would not strengthen this electromagnet.
Incorrect: fewer turns and lower current are not the changes given for increasing strength.

options: A low-current input circuit activates a high-current circuit.
A high-current input circuit activates a low-current circuit.
It permanently joins two circuits with no electromagnet.
It stops all current whenever the switch is turned on.
mcqs.stem: How does a magnetic relay use an electromagnet?
rationales: Correct: the low-current input circuit activates another circuit that works with a high current.
Incorrect: this reverses the relay's described input and output circuits.
Incorrect: a relay works with an electromagnet that attracts an iron armature.
Incorrect: turning the relay on makes the contacts join and turns on the high-current circuit.

options: It attracts the armature so that it detaches from the copper strip.
It increases the current without limit.
It makes the copper strip melt intentionally.
It keeps the circuit switched on.
mcqs.stem: What does a circuit breaker's electromagnet do when the current becomes excessive?
rationales: Correct: a sufficiently large current makes the electromagnet attract the armature away from the copper strip, breaking the circuit.
Incorrect: the circuit breaker is designed to switch the circuit off if the current is excessive.
Incorrect: the described action is the armature detaching from the copper strip, not the strip melting.
Incorrect: the circuit breaker switches off the circuit to protect appliances.

options: The diaphragm moves back and forth as the electromagnet's force varies.
The diaphragm stays fixed and blocks all sound.
The receiver uses a permanent magnet to switch off the microphone.
The diaphragm moves only when the current is constant.
mcqs.stem: How does an electromagnet help a telephone receiver produce sound?
rationales: Correct: varying current changes the electromagnet's force, making the diaphragm move back and forth to produce sound.
Incorrect: the section says the diaphragm moves back and forth.
Incorrect: the described receiver uses an electromagnet and a varying current.
Incorrect: it is varying current that changes the electromagnet's force and moves the diaphragm.

written.text: What is a circuit breaker? Describe its working with the help of a diagram.
written.finalAnswer: A circuit breaker is designed to pass a certain maximum current through it safely. If the current becomes excessive, it switches off the circuit. The current flows along a copper strip, through the iron armature and coil of the electromagnet. The electromagnet attracts the armature; if the current is large enough, the armature is detached from the copper strip and the circuit breaks.

steps.text: Take a battery of two cells, a switch, an iron nail, cotton (or plastic) covered copper wire, thread and a few paper clips.

steps.why: The coil is the part whose current produces the magnetic field that magnetizes the nail.
steps.text: Wind the wire over the iron nail to form a coil.

steps.why: The suspended coil can be connected to the circuit while the clips are tested near the nail.
steps.text: Suspend the coil by means of thread tied to its centre. Connect ends of the wire to the battery through the switch as shown in the figure.

steps.why: With the switch off, no current flows through the coil, so the nail does not act as an electromagnet.
steps.text: Keeping the switch OFF, bring some paper clips near to one end of the nail.

steps.why: Switching on current magnetizes the nail, which can then attract the clips.
steps.text: Now turn the switch ON and again bring the paper clips near to the end of the nail.

steps.why: Turning off the current shows that the nail's magnetism is temporary.

explain.title: What is an electromagnet?
explain.body: An iron nail or a rod becomes a magnet when an electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet. The current in the coil produces a magnetic field that magnetizes the iron.

explain.title: An electromagnet is temporary
explain.body: The iron object remains a magnet as long as electric current passes through the coil. When the current is stopped, it no longer remains a magnet.

explain.title: How to make it stronger
explain.body: Increasing the number of cells in the battery or increasing the number of turns of the coil increases the strength of the magnetic field. The stronger electromagnet can hold more clips.

explain.title: Devices that use electromagnets
explain.body: A magnetic relay uses a low-current input circuit to activate a high-current circuit. A circuit breaker switches off a circuit if current becomes excessive. In a telephone receiver, varying current changes the electromagnet's force and makes the diaphragm move back and forth to produce sound.

explain.title: Cranes and maglev trains
explain.body: A crane can lift iron and steel with a powerful electromagnet and release them by switching off the current. Maglev trains use magnetic forces to float above the guideway and use propulsion electromagnets to move forward.

mistakes: Do not say an electromagnet remains magnetic after the current is switched off; its magnetism is temporary.
Do not confuse increasing the number of cells or turns with decreasing the strength: either increase makes the magnetic field stronger.
When explaining a relay, keep the low-current input circuit and high-current circuit roles clear.
For a circuit breaker, do not say the electromagnet joins the contacts when current is excessive; it pulls the armature away so the circuit breaks.
In a telephone receiver, explain that varying current changes the electromagnet's force and moves the diaphragm.
